content.text:
Base directory for this skill: /Users/luke/.claude/skills/mac-health

# mac-health

Use Luke's `mac-health` wrapper before ad-hoc process spelunking.

Trigger aliases: `/mac-health`, `/mac-sweep`.

Ongoing optimisation programme: `~/Projects/personal/mac-resource-ops/VISION.md`.

## Tools installed

- `mac-health` — wrapper at `~/bin/mac-health`
- `btop` — interactive process/resource TUI
- `macmon` — Apple Silicon heat/power/GPU/ANE/RAM monitor
- `powermetrics` — Apple built-in deep sampler; requires sudo

## Quick commands

```bash
mac-health now              # one snapshot: heat, memory, disk, top CPU/RAM processes
mac-health watch            # opens btop for interactive app/process triage
mac-health heat             # opens macmon for heat/power/GPU view
mac-health heat-log 300 5   # CSV timeline for 5 minutes, every 5 seconds
mac-health heat-tail        # latest heat CSV path + last rows
mac-health history 60       # local CSV summary + SigNoz history query when API key is available
mac-health signoz-history 120 # SigNoz-only historical Mac health metrics
mac-health otel-emit        # emit one Mac health OTEL sample to local collector
mac-health record 180       # human-readable snapshots every 10s for 3 minutes
mac-health power            # sudo powermetrics deep thermal/power sampler
mac-health doctor           # workflow reminder
```

## Triage flow

1. For current + historical evidence, run:
   ```bash
   mac-health history 60
   ```
   This summarizes the latest local CSV and queries SigNoz historical metrics when `SIGNOZ_API_KEY`/keychain/1Password access is available.

2. If the Mac is lagging right now, run:
   ```bash
   mac-health heat-log 300 5
   ```
   Send/inspect the printed CSV path. It records CPU/GPU temperature, power, RAM/swap, and top CPU/RAM processes per sample.

3. For live visual process triage:
   ```bash
   mac-health watch
   ```
   Sort by CPU, memory, disk IO. Only kill obvious offenders.

4. For live heat/power view:
   ```bash
   mac-health heat
   ```

5. For broad evidence:
   ```bash
   mac-health record 180
   ```

6. For deep Apple thermal/power diagnostics:
   ```bash
   mac-health power
   ```

## SigNoz / OTEL history

Automatic emitter:

```bash
launchctl print gui/$(id -u)/com.lue.mac-health-otel
mac-health otel-emit
```

Historical query:

```bash
signoz-query mac-history --since 1h                 # API first, then ClickHouse fallback
signoz-query mac-history --since 1h --backend clickhouse
mac-health signoz-history 60
```

Metrics emitted to SigNoz include:

- `mac.heat.cpu.temperature`, `mac.heat.gpu.temperature`
- `mac.power.cpu`, `mac.power.gpu`, `mac.power.system`
- `mac.usage.cpu`, `mac.usage.gpu`
- `mac.memory.ram.used`, `mac.memory.swap.used`
- `mac.process.top.cpu`, `mac.process.top.ram.rss`

Resource filter:

```txt
service.name = lue-macbook-health
host.name = Lukes-MacBook-Pro.local
```

If API auth fails, `signoz-query` falls back to the self-hosted SigNoz ClickHouse backend via `kube-exec`. If both fail, check `SIGNOZ_API_KEY`/keychain/1Password for API mode and `bermont-kube` access for ClickHouse mode.

## Reading heat logs

Latest heat log:

```bash
mac-health heat-tail
```

Important CSV fields:

- `timestamp`
- `cpu_temp_c`, `gpu_temp_c`
- `cpu_power_w`, `gpu_power_w`, `system_power_w`
- `cpu_usage_pct`, `gpu_usage_pct`
- `ram_used_gb`, `swap_used_gb`
- `top_cpu_command`, `top_cpu_pct`
- `top_ram_command`, `top_ram_rss_mb`

Interpretation:

- High CPU + normal temp → runaway app/process.
- Rising temp + high system power → sustained load / possible thermal constraint.
- High temp + lag but low top-process CPU → check GPU, swap, disk IO, or powermetrics.
- Swap high / memory pressure critical → RAM pressure; browsers/Electron/LLM tools are usual suspects.
- Disk nearly full / high IO → Spotlight, backups, Docker/OrbStack, builds, browser cache.

## Guardrails

- Do not run infinite logging without the user asking. Prefer bounded `heat-log 300 5`.
- Do not kill processes unless the user approves or it is obviously safe and requested.
- `powermetrics` needs sudo; ask/notify before using it.
- Avoid printing broad env output; it is irrelevant and can leak secrets.

lastPrompt: why is my laptop so hot / running under so much load currently?

aiTitle: Diagnose high laptop temperature and CPU load

content.text:
Got the full picture. Here's the verdict — no mystery, it's a pile of AI agent runtimes all running at once.

## Why it's hot

**Load average: 13.87 / 21.02 / 33.38** on a 12-core machine. The 15-min figure (33) means ~15 minutes ago you were at **~2.8× core capacity** — badly oversubscribed. It's dropping fast now (33→21→14), so the worst already passed. Still running ~1.2× cores.

**The CPU hogs, in order:**
| Process | %CPU | What it is |
|---|---|---|
| `warp-oss` (Rusty.app) | 54% | Your terminal (the warp fork) |
| `WindowServer` | 48% | UI compositing — high because lots of windows/agent output churning |
| `claude` ×3 | 25 + 9 + 9% | Three Claude Code instances |
| `pi` ×2 | 15 + 13% | Two pi coding-agent runtimes |
| `node` | 19% | Agent subprocess |
| Claude.app (desktop) | 11+6% | Claude desktop app |
| Codex.app | 5% | Codex desktop app |
| `codedb` | 5% | MCP code-intel server |

**Memory is the real squeeze:** 31G used, **12G in the compressor, only 451M unused, 2.5G swapped**. That's genuine pressure — when RAM's that tight, everything thrashes harder, which feeds the load.

**Heat:** CPU 78°C / 19.7W — warm-busy, *not* throttling (Apple Silicon throttles ~100°C). The fans are responding to sustained multi-agent load, not a thermal fault.

## Bottom line
You've got **3× Claude Code + 2× pi + Claude desktop + Codex desktop + codedb + the terminal** all live simultaneously. That's the load — concurrent agent swarm, not one runaway process. Load is already recovering on its own as jobs finish.

If you want it cooler now: close the idle agent sessions you're not actively using (each pi/claude is ~0.5–0.6G RSS and 13–25% CPU), and the Claude/Codex *desktop* apps if you're driving everything from the terminal anyway. Want me to list which PIDs look idle vs active so you can prune safely?

content.text:
This changes the answer. It's **not your agent work** — the heavy hitters have all been running **2h 22m** (full session) and they're idle desktop GUI apps spinning, not the CLI agents you're driving.

## The real culprits: idle Electron apps + terminal render loop

Look at what's actually burning CPU and how long it's been up:

| Process | %CPU | Uptime | Reality |
|---|---|---|---|
| `warp-oss` / Rusty terminal | **57%** | 1h13m | GPU render loop (live output/spinner repaint) |
| **Codex.app** (renderer+chronicle+app-server) | **~40%** combined | 2h22m | Desktop app idle-spinning |
| **Claude.app** (renderer+gpu+helper) | **~26%** combined | 2h22m | Desktop app idle-spinning |
| `Stats.app` | 9% | 2h16m | Your menu-bar monitor is itself a hog |
| `pi` (one instance) | 15% | 1h09m | The only real agent load |
| `claude` (this session) | 7% | **3 min** | Me, just now |

**The system daemons spiking are symptoms, not causes:** `WindowServer` 19%, `systemstatusd` 17%, `coreaudiod` 14%, `syspolicyd` 27%, `trustd` 12%, `mediaremoted` 6%. Electron renderers constantly repainting wake WindowServer; their telemetry/code-sign checks hammer syspolicyd+trustd; audio contexts keep coreaudiod hot. That's ~95% CPU of pure overhead from apps doing *nothing useful*.

## Why "not using much" still = high load

Two tells in the data:
1. **CPU is ~48% idle but load avg is 9–13.** No processes in IO-wait (D-state), and Spotlight/backup/indexing are all ~0%. So it's not disk-blocked and not a runaway compute job. It's **many chatty threads waking constantly** — animation frames, telemetry pings, repaints — from a dozen Electron/GPU surfaces. Bursty scheduling, not sustained work. Classic idle-Electron-swarm signature.
2. The actual *agent CLIs* (pi, claude) are a minority of the load. **The desktop wrappers around them are the problem** — Codex.app and Claude.app together idle at ~66% CPU whether or not you touch them.

## Fix
Quit the **Codex and Claude desktop apps** if you're working from the terminal anyway — that alone reclaims ~1.4 cores. **Stats.app** at 9% is worth dropping too (use `macmon`/`mac-health` on demand instead of a permanent menu-bar drain). The terminal's 57% is the live render of whatever's scrolling — it'll settle when output stops.

Want me to quit the Codex + Claude desktop apps and Stats.app for you? That's the bulk of it.
